analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans import cheaper prescription drugs from Canada and other countries.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 243-186, but the Senate never voted and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Health and Human Services Secretary to write rules letting individuals, not just pharmacists and wholesalers, bring prescription drugs in from other countries where they sell for far less. It required imported drugs to be FDA-approved and to carry counterfeit-resistant packaging like the security features on US currency. The House passed it, but the Senate never acted.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions, especially seniors paying cash prices that can be many times higher than the same drug costs in Canada or Europe. The bill's own findings cite CBO estimates that seniors would spend $1.8 trillion on drugs over ten years and claim consumers could save hundreds of billions a year [S4]. Pharmacists and wholesalers, who could already import under prior law, gain a larger market, and companies making currency-style security packaging gain a new mandate [S2][S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers who fill prescriptions, especially seniors

how_it_helps.text: Directs the HHS Secretary, within 180 days of enactment, to issue regulations letting 'qualifying individuals' — anyone who is not a pharmacist or wholesaler — import covered prescription drugs, on top of the pharmacists and wholesalers current law already allows [S2][S3][S4].
Removes the sunset date on the importation provisions, making the pathway permanent rather than temporary [S2][S3].

Requires prescription drug packaging to incorporate counterfeit-resistant technologies similar to those the Bureau of Engraving and Printing uses to secure US currency, with drugs lacking them treated as misbranded [S3][S4].

Requires imported drugs and the facilities that make them to be FDA-approved and excludes pharmaceutical narcotics, and directs a study comparing the rate of misbranded or adulterated imported shipments with domestically transported drugs [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose US prices are the world's highest and who lose the ability to keep Americans from buying the same medicines abroad at lower prices [S4]. The pharmaceutical industry also bears the cost of adding approved security features to packaging for drugs subject to the requirement [S4]. Public-health critics bear the burden of arguing the safety case, since the bill narrows certain testing and record-keeping requirements for individual importers [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill relaxes safeguards for individual imports: authenticity and degradation tests are not required unless the importer is a wholesaler, and the Secretary no longer must track the original source and lot amounts for covered products [S2][S3]. Opponents, including FDA officials at the time, argued individual importation cannot be verified as safely as the domestic supply chain.

The savings figure in the bill — at least $635 billion a year — is a congressional finding, not an independent estimate, and the ultimate savings would depend on how the Secretary writes the regulations and whether foreign suppliers choose to ship to Americans [S4].

The actual savings depend on implementation details left to the Secretary's regulations, and drug companies could have restricted supply to Canadian pharmacies, limiting the volume of cheap imports in practice — a limit the bill does not address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of Americans paying the highest drug prices in the world, the potential savings were large and the mechanism — buying the same FDA-approved drugs abroad — is one Americans already attempt informally. The main honest cost is a safety trade-off: loosened testing and source-tracking for individual imports raise some counterfeit risk, though the bill offsets this with a currency-style packaging mandate. On balance the consumer benefit outweighs the safety risk, but the bill left significant design questions to future regulations.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 243-186 in July 2003, but the Senate referred it to its Health committee, which never acted, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced June 11, 2003, the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, but it never received a committee markup; instead it went straight to the floor under a special rule [S6].

A Democratic motion to recommit the bill to committee failed on a voice vote, and the House passed the bill 243-186 on July 25, 2003, with 155 of 205 voting Democrats, 87 of 229 voting Republicans, and the lone Independent in favor [S6][S7].

The Senate received the bill the same day and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never reported it, and the Senate never voted on it before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers came out ahead: they kept American patients paying US prices instead of world prices, and the bill died without a Senate vote despite a bipartisan House majority.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept US prices

against.what_they_did: Ran a major campaign against drug importation, arguing it could not guarantee drug safety and would undermine funding for research.

sides.party_line_note: Democrats largely backed the bill (155-45) while Republicans split against it (87-141); the partisan divide widened in the Senate, where the Republican majority never acted.

industries.note: Reimportation would have exposed their highest-priced market — the US — to competition from the same drugs sold cheaper abroad, eroding US prices and profits. Their loss is consumers' gain on prescription costs.

The bill mandates overt, currency-style counterfeit-resistant technologies on prescription drug packaging and treats noncompliant drugs as misbranded, creating a federal requirement for their products.

They already had importation rights under prior law, and the bill keeps their privileged position: individual importers face lighter testing duties, while wholesaler-level tests and records remain. A wider import market expands their sourcing options.
